title: Yorkshire Pudding
subtitle: Puffed, crisp batter puddings for the Sunday roast
excerpt: Egg-rich batter poured into searing-hot fat and baked at very high heat until puffed, hollow, and deeply golden. The essential companion to roast beef. The recipe is almost foolproof once you know the rules.

recipe.sourceNotes: Yorkshire pudding was first recorded in 1747 in Hannah Glasse's The Art of Cookery Made Plain and Easy, though dripping puddings baked beneath the roasting meat predate this. It is a product of the north of England where beef dripping was plentiful and the pudding was originally served before the meat to fill up the family before the expensive joint appeared. The recipe has not changed: batter of equal volumes of flour, eggs, and milk or water, poured into very hot fat. Both temperature extremes matter: cold batter, smoking fat.

recipeTools.notes: 12-hole tin for individual Yorkshires, or a roasting tin for one large pudding.

content.text: Rest the batter for at least 30 minutes. The fat must be smoking hot before the batter goes in: if it is not hot enough, the puddings will not rise. Work quickly: fill each hole just over halfway. Do not open the oven door for the first 20 minutes. Cold batter into smoking fat is the only technique that matters.
Whisk the flour, eggs, milk, and salt together until smooth. Leave to rest for at least 30 minutes at room temperature. The batter should be the consistency of single cream.
Heat the oven to 230 C / fan 210 C / gas 8. Add a small amount of oil to each hole of a 12-hole tin. Put the tin in the oven for 10 to 15 minutes until the fat is smoking hot.

Working very quickly, fill each hole just over halfway with batter. Return to the oven immediately. Bake for 20 to 25 minutes until puffed and deep golden. Do not open the oven door during the first 20 minutes. Serve immediately.
